prompt: I run a well drilling company out in the country, Harrow Creek Drilling. Never had a real logo, just the name painted on the trucks. Can you make one? Give me a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and inline SVG, system fonts only, no external assets, showing the logo so I can see what it looks like.
rubric: The mark is built around one specific idea tied to drilling, water or this place, not a stock water drop, generic circle or arbitrary swoosh.
The company name is legible and set deliberately as part of the mark, with a clear weight and letter shape rather than a default-looking text line.
The page also shows the logo at a small size (about 32 to 48px) or in a single flat color, and the mark still reads in that form.
Only a small number of colors are used and the palette suits a rural trade business instead of tech-startup gradients.
The page is a single self-contained file with no external fonts, images or scripts, and the logo is the clear focus of the page.

prompt: We're Larkspur Payroll, three years old, about 40 people. Our current logo is a rounded sans wordmark with a purple-to-teal gradient swoosh over the L. Prospects keep treating us like a scrappy startup and we sell to firms with 500+ employees. Redo the identity so we look more established. Put "Established 1998" under the name, since clients trust older companies. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS and SVG, system fonts, no external assets. Show the logo plus a business card and an email signature using it.
rubric: The new mark is visibly more restrained and confident than a gradient swoosh, and rests on one distinct idea rather than a pile of decoration.
The page does not print "Established 1998" or any other invented founding date, and the response or page says why a date the company cannot back up is a bad idea.
The business card and the email signature both show the same mark and the same type treatment, so they read as one system.
Text on the card and signature is readable at a realistic size and does not rely on gradients or tiny light-on-light type.
The identity uses a small, controlled set of colors and fonts that suit a serious B2B finance buyer without looking like a generic bank template.

prompt: Our bakery is called Crumb & Co. Our logo has a script wordmark in dark brown, a little wheat stalk drawing on the left, a cream-and-pink banner behind it, a gold outline around everything, and a tagline in tiny caps underneath that says "baked fresh with love since our first loaf". We use it on boxes, our shop sign and Instagram. People say it looks like every other bakery. What's going on and what would you change?
rubric: The critique names specific causes of the generic look drawn from the description (stock wheat symbol, stacked decoration, script plus banner plus outline), not only a vague call to be more unique.
It identifies at least one practical problem at small size or in one color, such as the thin tagline, the fine outline or the banner, on boxes or an avatar.
It proposes one concrete distinctive direction for the mark rooted in something about this bakery or its name, and says what to remove.
It says what is worth keeping, so the answer is not a blanket rejection.
Findings are ordered so the biggest problem comes first, and the answer ends with clear next steps instead of a long list of equal items.

prompt: Pinegate Hardware has been on the same corner for 41 years. Our sign and bags are just the name in a heavy slab serif, all caps, in a safety-orange on white, and a plain black version for receipts. Everyone in town knows it. Our new marketing hire says we need to rebrand because it "looks dated" and wants a modern sans-serif and a gradient icon. I'm not sure. Should we?
rubric: The answer takes a clear position, and that position is to keep the existing identity rather than replace it.
It names what is already working, such as local recognition, the strong single color, the sturdy wordmark and the black one-color version.
It limits any suggested changes to small, specific refinements (for example spacing, consistent use or one missing format) rather than a redesign.
It explains why a modern sans and a gradient icon would not fix a real problem, and what real evidence would justify a rebrand instead.
The answer is not padded with a full redesign proposal or a long list of new concepts.

prompt: I own a vet clinic. Twelve years ago my friend's kid drew our logo: a wobbly pencil sketch of a dog with one ear up, with the clinic name in a rounded font next to it. People in the neighborhood know the dog. We're opening two more locations next year and my business partner wants a clean new professional logo for all three. I'd hate to lose the dog. Refine it or replace it? Pick one and tell me what you'd actually do.
rubric: The answer commits to refine or replace rather than listing both without choosing.
The decision is argued from the clinic's situation, namely twelve years of neighborhood recognition and the move to three locations.
It says concretely what would change and what must stay, for example redrawing the dog with the same ear and posture, or tightening the name lettering, so a designer could act on it.
It covers how the mark will hold up in practice, for example as a small avatar, on a sign, or in one color across several locations.
It addresses the partner's concern about looking professional with something better than a vague reassurance.

prompt: Southbank Reading Room is a small neighborhood nonprofit library. Our mark is a stack of three books that also forms a letter S, with the name set beside it. We need to use it in a wide website header, a square social avatar, a narrow bookmark, and a canvas tote bag. How should the logo be arranged in each place? Describe the versions so our volunteer designer can build them.
rubric: The answer defines distinct versions (such as horizontal, stacked and mark-only) and says which one goes in the header, avatar, bookmark and tote.
The mark-only or compact version is specified for the avatar, with a note on what is dropped so it stays readable at small size.
It gives usable rules for protecting the logo, such as clear space around it and a minimum size below which the full lockup should not be used.
It covers the tote bag as a one-color print case and says how the mark holds up without color or fine detail.
The answer is organized per placement so the volunteer can follow it without further questions.

prompt:
Here's the SVG for our climbing gym logo, Boulderline. Can you clean it up a bit? Don't redo it, I like the idea.

<svg viewBox="0 0 320 120" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="g" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="1"><stop offset="0" stop-color="#ff5a36"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#ffd23f"/></linearGradient>
    <filter id="s"><feDropShadow dx="3" dy="3" stdDeviation="2" flood-color="#000" flood-opacity=".5"/></filter>
  </defs>
  <path d="M10 100 L45 30 L65 62 L82 40 L112 100 Z" fill="url(#g)" stroke="#222" stroke-width="1" filter="url(#s)"/>
  <path d="M25 100 L45 58 L58 80" fill="none" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="1"/>
  <circle cx="45" cy="30" r="4" fill="#ff5a36"/>
  <text x="128" y="72" font-family="Papyrus, fantasy" font-size="34" fill="#222" letter-spacing="1">Boulderline</text>
  <text x="130" y="96" font-family="Arial" font-size="8" fill="#888">INDOOR CLIMBING & TRAINING</text>
</svg>
rubric: The mountain-ridge idea and the Boulderline name are kept; the answer does not replace the concept with a new one.
It fixes problems that would show up in use, such as the drop shadow, the gradient, the hairline strokes and the tiny gray tagline, and gives the reason for each.
It addresses the font choice, replacing the fantasy-style face with something that reads well and does not depend on a font the viewer may not have.
It provides revised SVG or exact, specific changes the user can apply, not just general advice.
It says or shows that the cleaned-up version works in a single solid color and at a small size.

prompt: Our logo looks great on the website and in the PDF deck, but the 32px browser tab icon is a gray smudge and the embroidered polos came back with the fine lines melted together and the little tagline unreadable. Our designer says it's "just how embroidery works." Is that true? Why does this happen and what do we do about it? We're a small accounting firm, so we don't need a huge project.
rubric: The explanation says the designer is partly right but that the logo itself is the real problem, and names what in a detailed logo fails when reduced or stitched.
It gives concrete causes such as thin strokes, small gaps, tiny text, low-contrast color pairs or gradients, and ties them to the tab icon and the embroidery.
It recommends a simplified small-size or stitch version of the mark rather than shrinking the full logo, and says what to remove.
The advice is scaled to a small firm, with a short list of the few versions to make instead of a full identity overhaul.
It suggests a quick test the firm can run, such as viewing the logo at tiny size or in one flat color before ordering more items.

prompt: We named our internal analytics tool Quokka. It's only used by about 30 people on our team, and I just need a simple wordmark for the login page and the top of the wiki page, nothing fancy. Quick one please. Single self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: The page shows one clean wordmark option in a simple, readable treatment and does not present a sprawl of concepts, mascots or brand guidelines.
The name "Quokka" is spelled correctly, large enough to read, and set in a system font stack with a deliberate weight and spacing.
Color is minimal, with one main color on a plain background, and nothing decorative competes with the name.
The scale of the work matches the request: little or no explanation, no rebrand strategy and no long lists of questions.

prompt: Quick one, 60 words max please. Our craft brewery has a bear mascot, a crest with hops, and a wordmark. Should we cram all three into the logo so it shows everything we are?
rubric: The answer is 60 words or fewer.
It gives a direct answer, not a hedge, and says not to put all three into one logo.
It gives one concrete way forward, such as choosing one as the primary mark and assigning the others to specific uses.
It gives a reason a reader can check, such as how a crowded logo reads on a can or small label.
